document.abstract: There are many goals in the world of digital image manipulation. A few years ago, it was thought that real-time film manipulation would be a long way off. The push for the many DTV resolutions has caused many to dream of digital film mastering and “publishing” to the respective distribution formats. But, handling film in a manner that is common place for standard resolution video requires an understanding and appreciation of the acquisition, movement, processing/manipulation, previewing, and handling various output or data “publishing” methods. What does it mean to have a system and applications that are scalable and support scalable resolutions so that the artist “could” use similar systems for standard resolution through film resolution work? How close are we?

authors.bio: Kirk Law is a Sr. Director of Engineering at Silicon Graphics Computer Systems. He is responsible for Digital Media technology as applied to Silicon Graphics' Unix based workstations and servers as well as for Digital Media technology applicable to the company's NT products. He has been involved with many Digital Media architectures for solutions from Silicon Graphics. He joined Silicon Graphics in 1987, and has been involved in ASIC, Board, System Software, and Developer aspects of the companies solutions. Prior to joining Silicon Graphics, Mr. Law spent 4 years at the David Sarnoff Research Center in Princeton, New Jersey, where he was co-author on several patents in the area of digital TV processing. Mr. Law received two degrees from Purdue University in West Lafayette, Indiana. The first, in 1981, a Bachelor of Science from the School Electrical Engineering. The second, in 1983, a Master of Science from the School of Electrical Engineering.
